paragraphs.source_en: The hunter-gatherer year is divided into two phases–a period of concentration and a period of dispersion, and it is characteristic not only for the ! Kung but for most of the world's hunters and gatherers. This patterning is influenced by the nature of the ecology demanding flexibility in ! Kung living arrangements. During years of higher rainfall and numerous water holes the ! Kung have a greater range of options and could live in a large area in smaller groups. This phase is called private life (dispersion). But in drought periods only few water holes are available and all groups, previously spread, concentrate around them. This phase is called the public life (concentration), since a single large group exists in a region (Lee 1979).

units.source_en: This phase is called the public life (concentration), since a single large group exists in a region (Lee 1979).

paragraphs.source_en: Although the public phase is dictated partly by the ecology, living together in large groups has many social benefits for the ! Kung. This is the period of the year when social life is more intense, and during which occur many social activities, such as large-scale trance dancing and healing, initiations, trading, storytelling, and marriage arrangements. Another activity of the public life are the ! Kung men's initiation camps held around every seven years. At least seven boys of the correct age are needed to make the elaborate six week long initiation program and the boys' families camp together and provide food for the initiation camp. In years when no initiations are held in a local area, the initiates and their families often travel 70 to 100 km to join initiation camps at distant points (Lee 1979).

paragraphs.source_en: Lee (1979) notices that even in the years when initiation camps were not formed the concentration of groups included around 100 individuals or more. The trance dancing and healing ceremonies brought together medicine men from far and the healing medicine was thought to be especially effective when many performers entered trance at the same dance.

paragraphs.source_en: A concentration of San groups in rock art sites is attested in the Kalahari Desert (Van der Post 1958). In a fixed period of the year and travelling from large distances, these groups meet in the sacred hills of Tsodilo. It is a place of special significance to the San who believe that the hills are a resting place for the ancient powerful spirits and of gods who are believed to have produced the local rock paintings. The groups united there may seek spiritual strength and healing.
